worktree.//: baseRef 'head' branches a worktree from local HEAD rather than origin/<default>. Work here lands on a local feature branch before it is ever pushed, so the 'fresh' default silently seeds a worktree agent from a commit predating everything in progress -- it looks healthy and researches the wrong tree.

permissions.//: Precedence is deny -> ask -> allow, first match wins; specificity is ignored. Anything matching none of the three falls back to defaultMode. That is why the ask rules below still prompt even in acceptEdits.
permissions.//posture: Allow the harmless broadly, deny the dangerous explicitly. An unattended agent that hits a prompt stalls with nobody to answer it, so anything read-only, text-munging or repo-local is pre-approved rather than enumerated grudgingly. What must never happen is in deny, where it fails fast and unambiguously instead of stalling: the hardware recipes, ssh/scp (the raw path to the Jetson that denying those recipes does not cover), history rewriting, rm -rf and curl. Note rmdir is allowed but rm stays in ask -- rmdir only removes empty directories, so it cannot destroy work.
permissions.//unattended: The just recipes above are granted individually rather than as Bash(just:*), because a blanket grant would also cover move-arm, clocksync-check and deploy-robothost -- which command the physical JetRover arm and require a human watching for clearance. Those three are in deny, so an unattended agent cannot run them whatever its prompt says; robot/README.md logs three real arm-strain incidents. Prose in an agent definition is guidance; this is enforcement.
permissions.//web: WebSearch/WebFetch are in allow rather than ask so an unattended research run does not stall on a prompt. Bash(curl:*) stays in deny, and that is a distinction rather than an inconsistency: these two are constrained read-only fetches, curl is a general-purpose network tool. What a source may and may not be used for is in .claude/agents/deep-researcher.md -- a published number never enters results/ and never settles a comparison.
permissions.//git: Git is pre-approved wholesale (Bash(git:*)) rather than enumerated, because an unattended run that stalls on `git add` helps nobody and the genuinely destructive verbs are already in deny: --amend, rebase, reset --hard, filter-branch, push --force. Merging is the deliberate exception and stays in ask -- `git merge` and `gh pr merge` are how work reaches main, where the other machine sees it, and that is a decision rather than a step. Note precedence is checked tier by tier, so these ask entries beat Bash(git:*) even though they are narrower; per the note above, specificity is ignored. gh is granted per subcommand instead, because it reaches past the repo: gh pr create/view/list/diff/checks/status are pre-approved, while repo, release, auth, secret and api still prompt. Removing the prompt from push and PR-open removes the safety net, not the root CLAUDE.md rule that both happen only when asked.
